Anglin on identifying as alt-right vs identifying as NatSoc. (let's stir up some controversy and debate)

As someone who does identify more with the NatSoc principles than the more Americans style so-called 'racist liberal', I think Anglin is fundamentally right on a number of points and he outlines the reasons fairly well.

1.) Respect His first reason is fundamentally one of the most important and most overlooked ones. It always irked me to see neo-nazi groups trying to wear the SS or brownshirt uniforms because it's fundamentally disrespectful on a deep level. I refer to these people as 'costume nazis' and they have been one of the most destructive plagues on our movement in recent times (and I fundamentally think this was a mistake on Rockwell's part, a man I greatly admire). If you join a group and the people in it want to start wearing SS uniforms, get the fuck out because you're in a LARP group and not a serious political movement. I do think that holding great admiration for that uniform and its aesthetics is great and productive, but the reality is that none of us are worthy of that uniform. Seeing 12 overweight middle age balding dudes in a parking lot marching (poorly) wearing the brownshirt uniform isn't inspiring it's fucking pathetic. I support using it in online propaganda, I support 'redpilling' people on the second world war and the German National Socialist movement because even if they don't fully agree, they'll start understanding the modern world better and at the very least it will make people stop cowering in the corner when someone calls them a 'nazi'.

2.) Historical Context His second reason is kind of 'PR cucking' in a different way, but this particular quote:

I am entirely opposed to edginess for the sake of edginess

Is one of the funniest things Anglin has ever said. I'm with you on most of the post here Anglin but to say that with a straight face is just silly. It's as if you've never visited your own website. Your last post had a picture of a girl with cum all over her face with some quote about national socialism on it. But as far as socialism and the American right goes, he might have a point (I don't think this is at all the case in Europe). Fascism/National Socialist philosophy always dictated that a fascist uprising would be an expression of the fundamental core 'spirit' of that nation. The American spirit is one of tough individualism settling an untamed land. The German spirit is one of fighting for centuries to unify your people and then successfully doing so under a strict Prussian military command, massive industrialization through central economic planning and having to fight the entirety of Europe repeatedly just to stay alive (and this was BEFORE Hitler). There was a great unity in the German people, and the British naval blockade, the massive inflation and the total destruction of the German economy made a number of the 'socialist' elements in NatSoc not just economic theory but moral necessity. The alternative was letting millions of your own people starve. The free market wasn't going to fix it because the entire German economy was rigged by the Jews and the foreign allied governments. I believe this is going to be the case in America going forward and that, fundamentally, a mixed market NatSoc system will be the solution but that's not a pressing debate. I can "I told you so" post if that day does come.

3.) Freshness

Another major point. Let's even take Hitler as an example. At the time the German right was dominated by groups that wanted to revive the second German Reich and reinstate the kaiser. Even many top German generals wanted this (Rommel being one of the more prominent ones). Hitler took a different route. The party was new, the political system was new, the symbolism was 'new-ish' (the swastika is ancient, but it hadn't been part of German politic or society for millennia). The point isn't to try to revive a dead past. It is to take the timeless elements of your society's vision and create a new vitalism. The German National Socialists greatly revered the old Reich, but they didn't bother themselves with trying to carry the weight of a dead society on their backs. Take the ideals and carry them forwards, not try to wish for the past.

4.) Hitler is Dead

Not just Hitler. It's even further than that. During the Nuremberg trials some people remarked that the Nazi leaders weren't particularly brilliant or interesting but that is extremely difficult to believe. Given that most of them had genius or near-genius level IQ it's even more difficult to believe. The reality is that Hitler was the avatar of the movement but the people running the day to day operations were brilliant in their own right. There is no blueprint to recreate that as a political system. As a philosophy and set of guiding principles, absolutely. But that particular society is never coming back. It had as much to do with the specific people involved as it did any political platorm. I mean the 25 point platform of the NSDAP was never even endorsed by Hitler and he didn't particularly like some of the points. While the philosophy of the movement hit on some timless truths about not just our world, but the nature of life itself, the specifics of the party decisions were largely ways of implementing those truths to a specific time and place in the world. A time and place that we look back on longingly but which no longer exists.

There is a danger in re-branding, because it's easier for subversive elements to shift discussion away from the truth once re-branding happens. There are elements within the Alt-Right that twist truth, censor truth, or omit truth.
